storm.summary_layperson: Thunderstorms with heavy rain are moving through right now, and there's no protective buffer from the Sound this evening — the cove will see the same conditions as surrounding towns, with a Flood Watch in effect overnight.
storm.local_effect_blurb: The marine-layer buffer needs the Sound colder than the air, and today it's the opposite — air is already 6.5°F cooler than the 76°F water at 5 PM and the gap only widens through the night, so there's no cove-specific weakening effect at any point this window.
storm.detail_html:
NWS Upton's afternoon forecast discussion described an MCV interacting with a stalled boundary, the afternoon sea breeze, and a high-moisture (high-PWAT) airmass to produce heavy showers and embedded thunderstorms from late afternoon into the evening, with increasing flash-flood potential — a Flood Watch is in effect for the region until 2 AM. Current KOKX radar already shows that pattern playing out over the cove itself: the nearest storm core sits just 0.2 miles away at 59 dBZ, with half a dozen more cells in the 40–50 dBZ range within 3 miles, mostly arrayed to the north and west.

The instability profile is unusual — 0–6 km shear of 56–65 kt paired with modest CAPE (~300 J/kg, falling to near zero after sunset). That combination points to a shear-driven, low-CAPE heavy-rain event — embedded thunderstorms riding a boundary — rather than classic surface-based severe convection, consistent with the AFD's emphasis on flash flooding over damaging wind or hail.

The cove's usual local modifier isn't available tonight. The marine layer that sometimes blunts incoming storms only forms when Sound water runs several degrees colder than the air; today the Sound (76°F) is running warmer than the air (~70°F), an already-inverted gap that widens to roughly -16°F by 1 AM as the air cools overnight. There is no protective buffer at any point in this window. The sea breeze — which can sometimes oppose an approaching cell — never built today either (only 10% of coastal stations show a southerly component), so there's no wind-based discount available either.

The nearest closing storm cell is tracked 2.2 miles west of the cove, closing slowly (4.1 kt closing speed against an overall storm motion of 15.9 kt), with an estimated arrival around 6:11 PM. It arrives with neither local discount applied — expect it at full strength.

What would change the call: if the boundary lifts north before reaching the coast, or the MCV interaction weakens faster than modeled. Given the number of additional cells visible to the northwest, a training-storm pattern — repeated rounds moving over the same area — is plausible into the evening, which is the classic setup behind the flash-flood language in tonight's forecast discussion.

arrival.blurb: Radar-tracked cell 2.2 mi W closing slowly on the cove, arriving after sunset's marine layer never had a chance to form — expect it at full strength, with more cells likely to follow.

wind.regime_label: Light gradient wind — no sea breeze, direction may wander

hourly.shift_note: storm cores nearby, gusty and unsettled

wind.tactics_blurb: Storms sitting almost directly over the cove early in the window make this a stay-off-the-water call until the cell clears around 6:15 PM; once it does, an offshore N-NNE breeze fills to 13-14 kt by 9-10 PM, but that direction is the puffiest, shiftiest one this cove sees — play the shifts, don't trust any single header.
wind.tactics_detail_html:
Both sea-breeze ingredients fail today, so this is a gradient-only wind day, not a sea-breeze day. The air–water temperature difference is only 1.2°F by the simple measure and actually runs negative (air cooler than water) by the fetcher's fuller accounting — nowhere near the ~5°F thermal threshold — and only 10% of coastal stations are showing any southerly component. With the gradient wind itself averaging just 4.1 kt across well-sited stations, this lands as a light gradient day.

Direction agreement across stations is unusually low (34%), well below what a normal light-air day would show. That's expected here: a boundary with embedded thunderstorms is moving directly through the course area, and RYC's own instrument is currently reading NNE 32° while the near-term model has it swinging toward due N. Treat any single direction reading with caution until the closing storm cell clears the area, expected around 6:11 PM.

Through the window: light and gusty (5 kt, gusting mid-teens) while the storm core is nearby over the first hour, building slowly to 8-9 kt by 8 PM as the cell moves off, then jumping to 13-14 kt by 9-10 PM as CAPE collapses to zero and the post-convective gradient reasserts itself. Direction holds in the N-NNE band throughout, with gusts staying elevated (15-19 kt) the whole window.

N-NNE is offshore over land for the cove's N-S opening — per the cove's geography, that's the puffiest and shiftiest direction it sees, with oscillations of 15-30° even on a calm gradient day. Tonight that character is compounded by the storm cell passing directly through the course, so expect it to feel worse than the raw speed numbers suggest.

Bottom line on safety: radar shows an active storm core essentially on top of the cove right now, with a Flood Watch in effect. The first part of this window is a lightning and heavy-rain call, not a wind-strategy one. Once the cell clears, the building 13-14 kt NNE breeze after 9 PM is raceable but still puffy — center-course positioning limits exposure to the biggest oscillations until a clearer pattern sets up.

data_caveats: Buoy 44040 / WLIS marine obs are 65 min old — treat over-water wind/SST readings as slightly stale.

Station wind directions disagree sharply (34% agreement) — an active boundary with embedded storms is moving through, so any single direction reading is unreliable until the closing cell clears (~6:11 PM).
Arrival-time confidence is medium — nearest cell's closing speed (4.1 kt) is much slower than the overall storm-motion estimate (15.9 kt), reflecting geometry uncertainty in a multi-cell cluster.
